sections.title: Cap and form
sections.text: Lactarius sphagneti (Fr.) Neuhoff is a small milkcap, usually with a cap 2–5 cm across. The cap starts convex or bell-shaped, then expands and becomes depressed in the centre, sometimes with a small papilla; the margin may become wavy. It is bay-brown to reddish, brick-red or orange-brown, often paler and yellow-brown toward the edge. The surface is shiny and finely striate at the margin when moist, then becomes matte as it dries.

sections.title: Gills, stem, flesh and latex
sections.text: The gills are cream with a rusty tint and run slightly down the stem. The short stem is bay-brown like the cap, sometimes slightly thickened toward the base and often whitish at the apex. The whitish flesh may become reddish-ochre beneath the cap skin, but does not change colour when cut. The latex is white, mild and unchanging; the smell is faint and pleasant. Orton’s description gives ellipsoid spores about 8–10 × 6.5–7.5 μm, with conspicuous warts and ridges.

sections.title: Habitat and taxonomic distinction
sections.text: This ectomycorrhizal species occurs among sphagnum mosses (Sphagnum) in wet, peaty conifer forests; the association is with conifer roots, not with the moss itself. Scottish collections were found in pine woods and often in groups. In Estonia it is recorded as very rare, in September. Index Fungorum and GBIF use the name Lactarius sphagneti (Fr.) Neuhoff; the French INPN catalogue cites “Neuhoff ex Gröger” and notes a bibliographic discrepancy. Note also the history of the species concept: Orton distinguishes L. sphagneti in Neuhoff’s sense from L. sphagneti sensu Moser, which he refers to L. lacunarum; this is not a current synonym of L. sphagneti.

sections.title: Similar species and caution
sections.text: Lactarius sphagneti can resemble other small reddish-brown milkcaps in wet habitats. Its often paler cap margin, white latex that remains white, and strongly ornamented spores help compare it with similar species, but several characters must be examined together. The Czech Mycological Society atlas classifies it as inedible and lists it as vulnerable on the Czech national Red List; that conservation status is regional and does not describe its global status. Do not eat a wild mushroom based on this page or an image.

traits: Small 2–5 cm cap, convex then expanded and centrally depressed, sometimes with a low papilla and wavy margin
Shiny, finely striate at the margin when moist, matte when dry; bay-brown, brick-red to orange-brown, often paler at the edge
Cream gills with a rusty tint, slightly decurrent; short bay-brown stem, often whitish at the apex
Whitish flesh with a reddish-ochre tint beneath the cap skin, unchanged when cut; white, mild, unchanging latex and faint pleasant smell
Ellipsoid spores about 8–10 × 6.5–7.5 μm, with conspicuous warts and ridges in Orton’s description
Ectomycorrhizal in peaty conifer forests among sphagnum; reported as very rare in Estonia in the published survey
safetyNote: The Czech Mycological Society atlas classifies this species as inedible. Historical descriptions of mild latex do not establish edibility. Do not eat any specimen based on this page or a photograph.
